query: Platinum-group metals can promote distinct reactions, and earlier PGM-based nanoscale catalysts showed strong activity, selectivity, and durability in complex catalysis. A representative catalyst was reported to perform particularly well in ethanol oxidation, which involves 12-electron and 12-proton transfers, but these performance reports did not establish a comprehensive causal explanation of its behavior during operation. Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs its catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Define an unnamed controlled change with a suitable baseline, the predicted observations, the reaction regime in which the hypothesis should apply or fail, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: The outstanding performance of the platinum-group metal catalyst in ethanol oxidation is driven by a high density of surface defect sites that modify the catalyst’s electronic structure (via a d-band center shift), thereby optimizing the adsorption/desorption energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates and reducing poisoning effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale platinum-group metal catalyst as synthesized, possessing a native distribution of surface defect sites.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal treatment to deliberately modulate the surface defect density (either by promoting defect healing to reduce defects or by quenching post-annealing to increase defects).
generation.conditions: Ethanol oxidation performed in an alkaline electrochemical cell under similar potential ranges that activate 12-electron transfer processes, ensuring comparable environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and distribution of surface defects (e.g., under-coordinated atoms, crystalline imperfections).
generation.mechanism: Surface defects modify the local electronic structure by shifting the d-band center of the catalyst. This shift alters the adsorption energies of ethanol and the key reaction intermediates, facilitating complete oxidation (involving 12-electron/12-proton transfer) while mitigating catalyst poisoning (e.g., by CO-type species) and enhancing durability over time.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts with an engineered higher density of surface defects will exhibit increased current densities, improved selectivity toward complete oxidation products, and better durability compared to samples with lower defect densities; conversely, reducing defect density will decrease performance.
generation.baseline: The unmodified platinum-group metal catalyst with its as-synthesized (native) defect density.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to govern ethanol oxidation under alkaline conditions and at potentials where intermediate poisoning is a concern. It may not apply under acidic conditions or for simpler catalytic reactions where the role of multiple electron/proton transfers is less critical.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of defect density on performance metrics remains uncertain, as does the possible interplay with alloy composition or other surface effects that might also influence the reaction mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of platinum-group metal catalyst samples: one set subjected to thermal treatments aimed at reducing surface defects (annealed slowly) and a second set processed to enhance defect density (rapid quenching or chemical etching post-annealing). Perform ethanol oxidation tests under identical alkaline conditions using cyclic voltammetry and chronoamperometry, and analyze product distributions via chromatography.
measurements: Selectivity (measured by the distribution of complete versus partial oxidation products)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the catalyst samples with engineered higher defect densities do not show significantly enhanced activity, selectivity, or durability compared to baseline samples, or if the reduced defect samples show similar or superior performance, then the hypothesis that surface defect-induced electronic modifications govern the superior ethanol oxidation performance is falsified.

Dendritic defect-rich palladium–copper–cobalt nanoalloys as robust multifunctional non-platinum electrocatalysts for fuel cells

Abstract: Recently, the development of high-performance non-platinum electrocatalysts for fuel cell applications has been gaining attention. Palladium-based nanoalloys are considered as promising candidates to substitute platinum catalysts for cathodic and anodic reactions in fuel cells. Here, we develop a facile route to synthesize dendritic palladium–copper–cobalt trimetallic nanoalloys as robust multifunctional electrocatalysts for oxygen reduction and formic acid oxidation. To the best of our knowledge, the mass activities of the dendritic Pd59Cu30Co11 nanoalloy toward oxygen reduction and formic acid oxidation are higher than those previously reported for non-platinum metal nanocatalysts. The Pd59Cu30Co11 nanoalloys also exhibit superior durability for oxygen reduction and formic acid oxidation as well as good antimethanol/ethanol interference ability compared to a commercial platinum/carbon catalyst. Octahedral gold-silver nanoframes with rich crystalline defects for efficient methanol oxidation manifesting a CO-promoting effect

Abstract: AbstractThree-dimensional bimetallic nanoframes with high spatial diffusivity and surface heterogeneity possess remarkable catalytic activities owing to their highly exposed active surfaces and tunable electronic structure. Here we report a general one-pot strategy to prepare ultrathin octahedral Au3Ag nanoframes, with the formation mechanism explicitly elucidated through well-monitored temporal nanostructure evolution. Rich crystalline defects lead to lowered atomic coordination and varied electronic states of the metal atoms as evidenced by extensive structural characterizations. When used for electrocatalytic methanol oxidation, the Au3Ag nanoframes demonstrate superior performance with a high specific activity of 3.38 mA cm−2, 3.9 times that of the commercial Pt/C. More intriguingly, the kinetics of methanol oxidation on the Au3Ag nanoframes is counter-intuitively promoted by carbon monoxide.
